title: What to eat
intro: One splurge, everything else low-friction. The anchor is Saturday dinner — everything else here is walk-in or a one-tap online booking, never a project. The one trap worth naming up front: Toyosu's famous Sushi Dai/Daiwa Sushi counters run 2–5 hour waits and will likely split a party of six into two seatings — skip the queue and use the market for browsing instead.

items.name: Nihonryori RyuGin
items.how: Overseas guests book through a Tokyo hotel concierge or an approved partner (e.g. My Concierge Japan) — no direct self-service reservation. October dates open Sept 1, 2026; have your concierge call at opening.
items.crowd_tip: Private Room 1 (6–8 seats) or Private Room 2 (5–8 seats) fit a party of six without splitting the group.
items.why: 3 Michelin stars — the trip's anchor dinner, and the only finalist confirmed to seat six in one room.

items.name: Ginza Ukai-tei
items.hours: Dinner last order 19:30 (kitchen to 21:30); closed Sundays + 2 Mondays/month
items.how: Genuine self-service English-language online booking — no concierge needed.
items.crowd_tip: Private rooms are free of extra charge for parties of 4+; a dedicated chef cooks tableside, and everyone orders the same course.
items.why: The anchor's low-friction fallback if RyuGin's Sept 1 booking window closes first — still Michelin-starred teppanyaki, with a confirmed group-of-6 precedent.

items.name: Aragawa
items.how: TableCheck online, credit card required to hold the reservation.
items.crowd_tip: ⚠ Total restaurant capacity is reported at only ≈22 seats (a press estimate, not an official figure) — a table for six is a large fraction of the room on a Saturday. Book as early as possible if attempting this instead of RyuGin.
items.why: Worth the Effort: independent critics rank it among the best steak experiences in Japan — a genuinely different, splurge-tier alternative if you'd rather have this than the anchor dinner.

items.name: Kobikicho Ohno
items.hours: Dinner 17:00–21:00 (drinks last order 20:00); no fixed weekly closure day, irregular ad-hoc closures — confirm for your exact date
items.how: Serves only ONE party per day — the whole restaurant is a single nightly seating, so there's no release-window date to wait for; contact as early as practical for Sat Oct 17 since another party could take the date first. Official site lists an English menu and English-speaking staff; card acceptance isn't confirmed on either the official site or its operator listing — ask when booking.
items.price: ≈¥15,000/person (Gurunavi operator estimate — the official site doesn't publish a fixed course price)
items.crowd_tip: The sole private room (horigotatsu, door + walls) seats 2–6 — a party of six fills it exactly, with zero buffer for a 7th guest.
items.why: Worth the Effort: a tea-kaiseki restaurant discoverable only through Japanese-language search, serving a single reservation a day — a genuinely exclusive alternative to RyuGin if the concierge booking doesn't come through, at real booking-friction cost (no self-service, capacity fits 6 with no margin).

items.name: Yakiniku Ushigoro
items.how: Self-service TableCheck booking, no concierge needed.
items.crowd_tip: 11 private rooms at this branch; reservations accepted for 1–8 people, so six is a normal booking, not an edge case.
items.why: A lower-key wagyu yakiniku night — good Monday dinner without RyuGin-level booking friction.

items.name: Uobei Genki Sushi
items.hours: 11:00 AM–11:30 PM daily, last order 11:30 PM
items.how: Tablet ordering, bullet-train plate delivery — no reservation accepted (or needed), fast even for a group.
items.price: Budget kaiten-zushi — plates from ¥105, premium items priced higher
items.why: The easiest possible group dinner for a jet-lagged arrival night — no booking, no wait to speak of.

items.name: Tsukiji Outer Market
items.hours: Best 6:30–9 AM before the late-morning peak; two independent local accounts note roughly half the stalls close on Wednesdays as well as Sundays
items.how: Graze stall to stall rather than one sit-down meal — the market's own site asks visitors not to move through the narrow lanes as one large group, so split into pairs or trios while browsing.
items.crowd_tip: 10 AM–1 PM is the most crowded window, with lines at the famous stalls; go earlier.
items.why: The wholesale tuna auction moved to Toyosu in 2018, but the food stalls here never closed — still the best casual grazing breakfast in the city.

items.name: Toyosu Market
items.hours: Public hours ≈5 AM–5 PM on operating days
items.how: ⚠ Closed most Sundays and all Wednesdays — no Wednesday falls in this trip, but confirm the exact October calendar closer to the date since the official closure grid wasn't machine-readable when checked.
items.crowd_tip: Skip Sushi Dai/Daiwa Sushi's counters — 2–5 hour waits, and a party of six will likely be split into two seatings. Browse the market itself instead and save the splurge sushi for Saturday.
items.why: Where the wholesale fish trade actually is now — pairs naturally with teamLab Planets, a few minutes away.

items.name: Torien
items.hours: Mon–Thu/Sun 11:30–23:30, Fri–Sat 11:30–23:45; closed only New Year's Day
items.how: 150 seats with floor rentals for 30+ people — one of the few Omoide Yokocho stalls that actually handles a group booking rather than 2–3 seats at a tiny counter.
items.why: The practical way to eat together at Omoide Yokocho as one group of six instead of splitting across several 6-seat stalls.

items.name: Ameya-Yokocho (Ameyoko)
items.how: ≈400 shops/stalls over 500m — pure grazing, zero reservation friction.
items.crowd_tip: Weekday mornings, especially before lunch, are calmest; weekends and the pre-New Year season get significantly more crowded.
items.why: A real working shopping street, not a themed tourist arcade — a relaxed last-morning food crawl before the airport.
